about: Western Front lines traced from public-domain source maps, each with the dates it shows for the time slider (showFrom, showTo), its source, method, control points and accuracy, so it can be checked or re-traced.

lines.name: Furthest German advance, September 1914
lines.description: How far the German armies reached before the First Battle of the Marne (5 to 12 September 1914), from north-east of Paris to the Swiss border. The source map's line runs off its western edge north-east of Paris, so the part from there to the sea is not shown. Around Verdun the source's line also takes in the German advance of 1916.

source.title: The Western Theatre of the European War, 1918 edition, by Prof. B. Barrecchia, published by the Société Editrice Géographique, Paris (scale 1:500,000)
source.holder: Harry S. Truman Library & Museum, M1236
source.rights: Public domain (Truman Library: unrestricted); published 1918, out of copyright in the US

lines.sourceLine: solid red: Extreme limit of the German invasion in 1914
lines.method: trace_m1236.py 1.0: the line's ink colour masked on the 3036 x 3401 px image of M1236, followed by a least-cost path through waypoints set on the ink, georeferenced with a 2nd-order polynomial from 23 town control points, simplified to 500 m (ETRS89-LAEA).

accuracy.note: Good at Europe or region scale; not for village-level zoom.

lines.name: Western Front, late 1914 to March 1917
lines.description: The front after the First Battle of the Marne, which changed little until the German withdrawal to the Hindenburg Line began on 16 March 1917. Its northern part formed during the race to the sea (September to November 1914). Battles at Ypres, Verdun and the Somme moved parts of it by a few kilometres. Near Ypres the source map shows only the later line, so this line runs further east of Ypres there than the front of 1915 and 1916.

lines.name: Western Front, March 1917 to March 1918
lines.description: The front after the German withdrawal to the Hindenburg Line (16 March to early April 1917), as the source map shows it in February 1918, before the German spring offensive of 21 March 1918. The 1917 battles of Arras, Messines, Passchendaele and Cambrai moved parts of it by up to about 10 km, so for spring to December 1917 it is approximate. A US Army map of the front on 21 March 1918 (Truman Library M549) agrees with it to within about 3 km.

lines.name: Western Front, 10 June 1918
lines.description: The front on 10 June 1918, after the German offensives of spring 1918 had pushed bulges towards Amiens (from 21 March) and to the Marne at Château-Thierry (from 27 May). The source map stops near Albert, so the front from there north to the sea, held by British and Belgian forces, is not shown.

source.title: Length of front occupied by Belgian, French, British and American forces, June 10, 1918 (US Army annotations on a French base map, 1:600,000). Map Room, G-3, General Headquarters, American Expeditionary Forces
source.holder: Harry S. Truman Library & Museum, M557
source.rights: Public domain (Truman Library: in the public domain and can be used freely); annotated by the US Army in 1918 on a French map published before 1929

lines.sourceLine: black ink line along the coloured bands (Belgian, French, British, American sectors)
lines.method: trace_truman_1918.py 1.0: the black front-line ink masked on the Truman Library image, followed by a least-cost path from end to end; M557 matched to M562 (same base map) by SIFT features and a 2nd-order polynomial (RMS under 0.6 px), then placed on the ground with an affine fit from 29 town control points on M562 (RMS 1.8 km), simplified to 500 m (ETRS89-LAEA).

accuracy.note: Good at Europe or region scale; not for village-level zoom.

check.where: all seven maps from June 10 to September 10; each map's median 1.4 to 2.0 km

lines.description: The front on 10 September 1918, two days before the American attack on the St Mihiel salient (12 September). The source map stops west of Cambrai, so the front from there north to the sea is not shown. Shown for ten days, like the other maps in this series; the next map used is 30 October.
